<reason>A very close, high-quality clash. CON (A) did the more intricate rebuttal work: the "triggerable yet sent home" tension, the bail-gatekeeper point, and forcing PRO to admit the motion only "implies" rather than requires safeguards were all real hits, and the Maryland doorway example genuinely dents "reversibility." But PRO (B) neutralized the central contradiction with a plausible timing answer (dangerous while armed, less lethal once disarmed), kept the motion's own text (judicial finding of credible imminent risk, temporary order) as its due-process floor, and used its pressure question to pin CON to an honest but costly position: if evidence falls short of arrest or a clinical hold, the guns stay. CON's reply that such evidence "isn't imminence" and that other tools always fit asserts away the gap rather than proving it, while PRO's suicidal-crisis-with-a-loaded-gun case makes the gap intuitively real. CON's "borrowed rifle and truck" follow-up was weaker than its original attack, and its Rebuttal 2 was clipped. PRO's closing gave the cleaner decision rule for a third-party reader—"possession until the first attempt"—so it edges the debate by a razor-thin margin.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A1 in Rebuttal 2 ([B4.1]–[B4.2]) answering CON's contradiction charge: notice is dangerous while the gun is in reach, sending him home is tolerable once it is not—"liberty is not a loaded gun." It defused CON's sharpest line and reset the debate to CON's uncomfortable admission that the guns stay whenever no other tool has fired.</best_rebuttal>
